hanushek.name: Evidence, Politics, and the Class Size Debate
hanushek.author: Eric A. Hanushek
hanushek.description: Eric Hanushek’s chapter in The Class Size Debate (2002), edited by Lawrence Mishel and Richard Rothstein, pages 37–65. It critiques class-size evidence and broad reduction policies.

claims.name: STAR-sized early-grade class reductions can be worth their cost.
claims.description: Krueger (2003) argues that modest achievement gains can justify reducing classes from 22 to 15 pupils in grades K–3. His earnings-based case is conditional on modeled returns, not observed lifetime benefits.
claims.locator: Section 3, F61; Section 2.2, Table 5, F56–F58; caveats F58–F59

claims.name: Counting studies equally strengthens the evidence that smaller classes improve achievement.
claims.description: Krueger (2003) finds that reweighting 277 estimates from 59 studies reveals a positive relationship obscured by counting every estimate equally. This is a contested literature interpretation, not a new experiment.

claims.name: Equal study weights do not resolve bias in class-size research.
claims.description: Hanushek (2002) argues that Krueger’s reweighting favors weaker estimates. He emphasizes omitted state policies and prior educational inputs when judging study quality.
claims.locator: Chapter 2, The importance of quality, printed pp. 46–50; conclusion p. 61

claims.name: STAR does not justify across-the-board class-size reductions.
claims.description: Hanushek (2002) argues that broad reductions are too costly for the benefits established by existing evidence. He allows that reductions can be worthwhile in particular circumstances.

claims.name: Projected earnings alone are too uncertain to justify large class-size reductions.
claims.description: Hanushek (2002) challenges the compounded assumptions connecting early test gains to lifetime earnings. He also argues that policy choices must consider alternatives such as improving teacher quality.

claims.name: STAR’s early gains do not establish benefits from smaller classes in later grades.
claims.description: Hanushek (2002) interprets STAR’s advantage as concentrated at initial entry into small classes. He disputes extrapolation to later grades or smaller reductions, rather than claiming that no students benefit.
claims.locator: Chapter 2, The Tennessee class size experiment, printed pp. 55–58

pairs.reason: The existing 6.2% conditional return supplies the economic argument; it is not an independent experiment.
The existing 4% discount/1% wage-growth scenario supplies the modeled benefit and cost comparison; it shares the return model.
Hanushek challenges relying on this modeled earnings case for investment; one-sided methodological rebuttal, not a denial of the calculation.
Forecast uncertainty and alternative investments underpin Hanushek’s broad-policy objection.
Limited extrapolation underpins the objection to across-the-board reductions.
Hanushek’s criticism of the underlying evidence supports his broad-policy conclusion.
A conditional early-grade economic case and an objection to uniform policies have different scope; they are not logical negations.
A changed pooled interpretation and a bias objection differ; no claim that reweighting did not change the numerical summary.
The literature interpretation gives context but does not itself establish economic value.
An initial kindergarten gain is compatible with Hanushek’s extrapolation objection; no forced opposition.
The experimental percentile-rank effect is relevant context, not the model’s separate 0.20-SD inputs.
